summary: 1931 gable-roofed L-4 on Wam Mountain, retired from fire detection in the 1950s and long a Recreation Rental, but Recreation.gov's listing now says it is no longer a rental.

facts.status_note: Recreation.gov's listing for the cabin now shows a notice reading 'No longer a rental'; whether the structure itself still stands and is otherwise accessible is not confirmed by the sources checked here.

access.note: Formerly bookable via Recreation.gov as a rental cabin; that listing now states 'No longer a rental,' with no explanation given. A short hiking trail (Wam Lookout Trail #339A) and a longer Pacific Northwest Trail approach both reach the site.

visit.trail_note: Reached by a roughly 0.3-mile trail (#339A) from a forest road, or via a longer route on the Pacific Northwest Trail; current rental/access status is unclear pending a Recreation.gov update.

events.note: Built as a gable-roofed L-4 cab, described by NHLR as one of the last of that style.
Last used for fire detection in the 1950s.
Listed on the National Historic Lookout Register as US 350 on May 12, 2000.
Recreation.gov listing now carries a 'No longer a rental' notice (observed as of this research date; no date given for when the change occurred).

evidence.supports: built 1931, gable-roof L-4, 7,121-foot peak, Whitefish Range, last used 1950s, survived due to remoteness
evidence.quote: One of the last gable roof L-4s, Wam Mountain Lookout was constructed in 1931 by the Forest Service atop a 7,121' peak in the Whitefish Range in Montana. Last used for fire detection in the 1950s, the lookout escaped destruction probably because of its remote location.

evidence.supports: 1931-vintage gable-roofed L-4, last used 1950s, restored for rental, patrol point 1 mile northeast
evidence.quote: This 1931-vintage gable-roofed L-4 cab was last used in the 1950's. It is listed on the National Historic Lookout Register, and has been restored and available on the Recreation Rental program. There was also a patrol point 1 mile northeast along the ridge.

evidence.supports: listing now shows it is no longer a rental

evidence.supports: recent storm damage closing roads/trails across the Kootenai National Forest
evidence.quote: Efforts continue across the Kootenai National Forest (KNF) on road, trail, and recreation site clearing after intense windstorms and flooding over the winter months heavily impacted the forest.

corrections.proposed: restricted — Recreation.gov listing now states the cabin is 'No longer a rental'
corrections.why: The brief's source_pages list the Recreation.gov rental page as still active, but the live listing has changed to show the cabin is no longer bookable. No reason or date for the change is given on the page.

notes_for_editor: Key open question: Recreation.gov's listing for Mt. Wam now says 'No longer a rental' with no date or reason. Worth a follow-up check closer to publication, and/or a call to the Eureka Ranger Station (406-296-2536, listed on the same page), to see whether this reflects storm damage, a permanent program change, or something else, and whether the structure is still standing and publicly reachable. Fact-check 2026-10-04: the story claimed 'other online trail guides describe a longer approach via the Pacific Northwest Trail from a road junction near Strahl Peak', citing the Hiking Project page (source 4); that page contains no mention of the Pacific Northwest Trail or Strahl Peak, and no other source in this file supports it, so the claim was removed from the story as unsupported.
